question.problem: Given that $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find $L\{u(t-7)({t}^{2}+2)\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
question.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-as}\,L\{g(t+a)\},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L\{u(t-7)({t}^{2}+2)\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=7,$ and we have 

$$
L\{u(t-7)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-7s}\,L\{g(t+7)\},
$$

where $g(t)={t}^{2}+2.$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+7) & =(t+7)^{2}+2 \\  & ={t}^{2}+14t+49\,+\,2 \\  & ={t}^{2}+14t+51.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t+7)\} & =L\{{t}^{2}+14t+51\} \\  & =L\{{t}^{2}\}+14L\{t\}+51L\{1\} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+14\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+51\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{51}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-7)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-7s}\,L\{g(t+7)\} \\  & ={e}^{-7s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{51}{s}).\end{aligned}
$$
